summary: Chino Airport is a general aviation facility in the Inland Empire region of Southern California, originally established in the 1940s as a military training base. Today it serves as a hub for private aviation, flight training, skydiving operations, and aircraft restoration, and is closely associated with the renowned Planes of Fame Air Museum located adjacent to the airfield. The airport has frequently been used as a filming location for Hollywood productions due to its variety of vintage and modern aircraft.
faqs:
Q: Does Chino Airport offer commercial airline service?
A: No, Chino Airport is exclusively a general aviation facility with no scheduled commercial passenger service. Visitors typically arrive via private aircraft, flight schools, or skydiving operators.

Q: Can I skydive at Chino Airport?
A: Yes, Chino is one of Southern California's most popular skydiving destinations, with tandem jumps available year-round through licensed operators based at the field.

Q: Is there an aviation museum at Chino Airport?
A: The Planes of Fame Air Museum is located directly adjacent to the airport and features one of the largest collections of flying WWII-era aircraft in the country.

Q: Who owns and operates Chino Airport?
A: Chino Airport is owned and operated by the County of San Bernardino, making it a publicly owned public-use airport.
transport_tips: The airport is most easily reached from the Pomona Freeway (CA-60) via Central Avenue exits in the city of Chino, with ample free parking available on-site for visitors and pilots. It sits roughly 35 miles east of downtown Los Angeles and about 10 miles southwest of Ontario International Airport, making it a convenient option for Inland Empire travelers. Rideshare services and rental cars are the most practical options since there is no public transit directly serving the airfield.
local_tip: If you visit for the Planes of Fame Air Museum, time your trip for one of their monthly Living History Flying Days, when many of the museum's rare warbirds actually take to the sky — a rare treat you won't find at most aviation museums.
